opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that turned out to be one of the most important details in the whole line of work on model zoos and hyper-representations. When you treat neural network weights as a data modality, you quickly realize they don't behave like images or text. Different layers live on very different scales. The weights in a first convolutional layer might have a completely different distribution than those in a final linear layer. If you train an autoencoder on the raw weights with a plain reconstruction loss, like mean squared error over the flattened vector, the loss is dominated by whichever layers have the largest magnitudes. The model learns to reconstruct those well and essentially ignores the small-magnitude layers.

That's a problem, because for the network to actually work you need every layer to be reasonably accurate. A small error in a layer with tiny weights can be relatively huge for that layer and can wreck the downstream function. So what we did was normalize per layer, standardizing each layer's weights using statistics computed across the model zoo. That puts every layer on an equal footing, so the reconstruction loss weighs them comparably. In practice, that made a big difference: reconstructed or sampled models went from performing near chance to performing close to the original models.

The other lesson was that low reconstruction error in weight space doesn't automatically mean high functional fidelity. Two weight vectors can be close in an L2 sense and behave quite differently, and vice versa, because of things like permutation symmetries and the nonlinear way weights map to function. So beyond normalization, we found it valuable to combine the reconstruction objective with other signals. Contrastive losses help the representation capture the structure of the zoo and the symmetries, and we used augmentations like permuting neurons, which give you functionally equivalent models with different weights. That pushes the encoder toward representing what the network does, not just the coordinates of its weights.

So the short version: normalization decides which parts of the network the model pays attention to, and the loss decides whether you're optimizing for looking right in weight space or for working in function space. Getting both right is what makes generated weights actually usable, whether for initialization, transfer learning, or sampling new models from the learned distribution.

fable-5.1.text:
That's really a central question for us, because when you move from training a network to generating its weights, the weights themselves become the data. And weight spaces are strange data. The values are tiny, they're distributed very differently across layers, and there are all these symmetries, permutations of neurons, scaling between consecutive layers, where many different weight vectors describe exactly the same function. So normalization and the loss are really where you decide what the generator is allowed to care about.

On the normalization side, we found early on that if you just take raw weights and feed them into an autoencoder or a diffusion model, the model spends most of its capacity on things that don't matter. A layer with large magnitudes dominates the reconstruction, the small layers get ignored, and you end up with something that looks close in weight space but behaves nothing like the original network. So we normalize, often per layer or per model, and in our hyper-representation work we also canonicalize the permutation symmetries, so that two networks that compute the same function actually land close together in the representation. Once you do that, the latent space starts to become meaningful. You can see training trajectories, you can see which models generalize, and sampling from it gives you weights that actually work when you put them back in a network.

The loss is the other half of the story, and there's a real tension there. A plain mean squared error on the weights is the obvious choice, and it's stable, but it treats every parameter as equally important, which is simply not true. Some weights you can perturb a lot without changing anything, others are extremely sensitive. So a low MSE can still give you a model that doesn't perform, and conversely, a reconstruction with a noticeable MSE can perform just as well as the original. That's why we moved towards combining reconstruction with contrastive objectives, and also toward evaluating fidelity in function space rather than weight space, so looking at the accuracy, or the agreement in predictions, of the generated model instead of just the distance to the source weights. In the end, that's what fidelity means for us: not that the numbers match, but that the behavior does.

astra-6.text:
They’re both very important, because generating weights is a little different from generating an image. With an image, you can tolerate some small pixel errors. With weights, a small error in the wrong place can change the behavior of the network quite substantially.

Normalization matters because the scales of the weights can differ across layers. If you reconstruct all of those weights with a single, unnormalized objective, the layers with larger values can dominate the loss. You might get a good reconstruction score overall while reconstructing another layer quite poorly. So you want a representation and a normalization scheme that allow the model to capture those differences without simply ignoring the smaller-scale weights.

And then there’s the question of what fidelity means. Does it mean that the generated weights are close to the original weights numerically, or that the resulting network behaves similarly? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. Different weight configurations can implement the same function. So weight reconstruction loss is useful, but ultimately you have to evaluate the generated network on the task. That’s where you see whether the information that matters has actually been preserved.

sol-6.1.text:
They matter quite a lot, because fidelity in weight space is not necessarily the same as fidelity in function space. You can reconstruct the weights with a small error and still change the behavior of the network substantially.

Normalization helps because different layers can have very different weight scales. If you use a reconstruction loss directly on the raw weights, the layers with larger values can dominate that objective. Normalizing gives the model a more balanced representation to learn, but you also have to preserve the information needed to recover those scales when you generate a network.

And then the loss defines what you mean by a good reconstruction. A weight reconstruction loss is useful, but ultimately we care about whether the generated network works. So I would look at both: how well we reconstruct the representation, and how well the resulting network preserves the behavior and performance of the original.
